pages.name: One step
pages.text: [[Euler's method]] solves a rule by walking it, so it works even where no formula exists. It reads the slope, walks a short straight step along it, then reads again. Each step lasts the same time, the [[step size]] `h`. Here the rule is `dV/dt = −V ÷ 1`, since `τ = RC` = 1 s. The faint marks are its [[slope field]]. The faint curve is the exact answer. At 12 V the slope is −12 V a second. Half a second along it takes you down 6 V, to 6 V.
pages.alt: Rule: d V by d t equals minus V divided by 1. tau equals RC equals 1 s. h equals 0.5 s. 12 plus 0.5 times ( minus 12) equals 6 V. A dot at 12 volts reads the slope arrow there and walks half a second straight along it, down to 6 volts. slope minus 12 V a second. 6 V.

pages.name: The next step
pages.task: Now you stand at 6 V, at 0.5 s. Where does the next 0.5 s step land?
pages.why: At 6 V the rule gives a slope of −6 V a second. Walk 0.5 s along it and you fall 0.5 × 6 = 3 V. So you land on 6 − 3 = 3 V. Each step is new value = old value + `h` × slope.
pages.alt: Rule: d V by d t equals minus V divided by 1. tau equals RC equals 1 s. h equals 0.5 s. 6 plus 0.5 times ( minus 6) equals 3 V. after 1 s. 6 V. 3 V.

pages.name: The drift
pages.text: Here are both 0.5 s steps beside the exact curve. At 1 s the walk reads 3 V. The curve reads 4.41 V. The hatched gap between them is the [[drift]], 1.41 V. The short ticks along the first step show the true slope as the voltage falls. It eases off. The step keeps the slope it read at its start. So it falls too far, and the walk drifts below the curve.
pages.alt: Rule: d V by d t equals minus V divided by 1. tau equals RC equals 1 s. h equals 0.5 s. Two half-second steps reach 3 volts at 1 second, below the curve's 4.41 volts. The 1.41 volt drift between them is hatched. Ticks along the first step show the true slope flattening while the step stays straight. curve 4.41 V. walk 3 V. drift 1.41 V. ticks: the true slope eases off.

pages.name: Smaller steps
pages.task: Start again at 12 V, with 0.25 s steps. Where is the walk at 0.5 s?
pages.why: The first step falls 0.25 × 12 = 3 V, to 9 V. At 9 V the slope is −9 V a second. So the second step falls 0.25 × 9 = 2.25 V, to 6.75 V. The exact curve reads 7.28 V there. One 0.5 s step reached only 6 V. So the smaller steps sit closer to the curve.
pages.alt: Rule: d V by d t equals minus V divided by 1. tau equals RC equals 1 s. h equals 0.25 s. 12 plus 0.25 times ( minus 12) equals 9 V. 9 plus 0.25 times ( minus 9) equals 6.75 V. after 0.5 s. 9 V. 6.75 V. curve 7.28 V.

pages.name: Step size
pages.text: Each step reads the arrow at its start and walks straight along it. The log keeps the value at 1 s for each step size, from 1 s down to 0.05 s. Shorter steps re-read the slope more often, so the drift shrinks. For small steps the drift is about in proportion to `h`. The price is work. Halve `h` and you take twice as many steps.
pages.alt: Rule: d V by d t equals minus V divided by 1. tau equals RC equals 1 s. h equals 0.05 s. Steps of 0.05 seconds. At 1 second the walk reads 4.30 volts, 0.11 volts below the curve. drift 0.11 V.

pages.name: Halve the step
pages.task: With 0.1 s steps the drift at 1 s is 0.23 V. What is it with 0.05 s steps?
pages.why: For small steps the drift is about in proportion to the step. So halving the step about halves the drift, and 0.23 V becomes about 0.11 V. The walk reads 4.30 V at 1 s, against the curve's 4.41 V. With 0.1 s steps the value at 1 s was about 5% low.
pages.alt: Rule: d V by d t equals minus V divided by 1. tau equals RC equals 1 s. h equals 0.05 s. 0.05 s steps: 4.30 V at 1 s, drift 0.11 V. drift 0.11 V.

pages.name: Too big a step
pages.text: Now the plot runs to 6 s, and below 0 V. The dashed line is the [[steady state]], 0 V. Each step adds `h × (−V ÷ τ)`. So each step multiplies the voltage by `1 − h ÷ τ`. With 1.5 s steps that factor is −0.5. So the walk swings either side of 0 V and dies away. The exact curve never crosses 0 V. Bigger steps swing harder.
pages.alt: Rule: d V by d t equals minus V divided by 1. tau equals RC equals 1 s. h equals 1.5 s. each step: V times (1 minus 1.5 divided by 1) equals V times minus 0.5. so the swing dies away. Steps of 1.5 seconds. Each step multiplies the voltage by minus 0.5, so the walk swings either side of 0 volts and dies away. steady state 0 V. minus 6 V. 3 V. minus 1.5 V. 0.75 V.

pages.name: One big step
pages.task: Take 1.5 s steps from 12 V. Where does the first step land?
pages.why: At 12 V the slope is −12 V a second. Walking it for 1.5 s falls 1.5 × 12 = 18 V. That goes straight past 0 V, to −6 V. The real voltage never goes below 0 V. So the swing comes only from the step.
pages.alt: Rule: d V by d t equals minus V divided by 1. tau equals RC equals 1 s. h equals 1.5 s. 12 plus 1.5 times ( minus 12) equals minus 6 V. steady state 0 V. after 1.5 s. minus 6 V.

pages.name: A tank
pages.text: A tank fills at a steady rate and drains through its base. The outflow grows with the square root of the depth. Its level `y` obeys `dy/dt = 0.3 − 0.2 √y`, in metres and minutes. It starts empty. It settles where `0.2 √y` = 0.3, so `√y` = 1.5 and `y` = 2.25 m, the dashed line. No tidy formula gives `y` against time, so there is no exact curve. Step it, then halve the step and step again. At 4 min each halving moves the answer less.
pages.alt: Rule: d y by d t equals 0.3 minus 0.2 root y. steps of 0.25 min. Steps of 0.25 minutes from empty. At 4 minutes the level reads 0.73 metres. steady 2.25 m. 4 min.

pages.name: One tank step
pages.task: The tank's level is 1 m. Where does one 1 min step take it?
pages.why: At 1 m, √y is 1. So the slope is 0.3 − 0.2 × 1 = 0.1 m a minute. One minute along it adds 0.1 m. So the level reaches 1 + 0.1 = 1.1 m.

pages.name: The coil, stepped
pages.task: The coil's rule is `di/dt = (24 − 10 i) ÷ 0.5`. From 0 A, take two steps of 0.01 s. What current do you reach?
pages.why: The starting slope is 24 ÷ 0.5 = 48 A a second. So after 0.01 s, `i` = 0 + 0.01 × 48 = 0.48 A. There the resistor takes 10 × 0.48 = 4.8 V. So the slope is (24 − 4.8) ÷ 0.5 = 38.4 A a second. After 0.02 s, `i` = 0.48 + 0.384 = 0.864 A. The exact formula gives 0.791 A. The walk runs high. This curve flattens as it rises, but each step keeps its steeper starting slope.
pages.alt: Rule: d i by d t equals (24 minus 10 i) divided by 0.5. steps of 0.01 s. 0 plus 0.01 times 48 equals 0.48 A. 0.48 plus 0.01 times 38.4 equals 0.864 A. the walk runs high of the curve. after 0.02 s. 0.48 A. 0.864 A. curve 0.791 A.

pages.name: Why it swings
pages.task: With 0.075 s steps, the coil's walk reads 0, 3.6, 1.8 and 2.7 A. Why does it swing?
pages.answer: The step is longer than τ, so it overshoots
pages.why: The coil's `τ` is 0.5 ÷ 10 = 0.05 s. A 0.075 s step is longer than that. Each step multiplies the gap to 2.4 A by 1 − 0.075 ÷ 0.05 = −0.5. So the walk jumps past 2.4 A and back, a little less each time. The real current climbs to 2.4 A without crossing it.
pages.alt: Rule: d i by d t equals (24 minus 10 i) divided by 0.5. steps of 0.075 s. gap times (1 minus 0.075 divided by 0.05) equals gap times minus 0.5. a step longer than tau overshoots. steady 2.4 A. 3.6 A. 1.8 A. 2.7 A. tau equals 0.05 s.
options: The step is longer than τ, so it overshoots

pages.name: What next
pages.task: At 4 min the tank reads 0.79 m with 1 min steps and 0.75 m with 0.5 min steps. What should you do next?
pages.answer: Halve the step again and compare
pages.why: One run cannot tell you its own drift. So halve the step and run it again. Steps of 0.25 min give 0.73 m. Each halving moves the answer less. When it barely moves, you can trust it.
